notes:
Area under a curve

  • Area bounded by $y=f(x)$, the x-axis, and lines $x=a,x=b$ (with $f(x)\ge0$): $A=\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
  • If part of the curve lies below the x-axis, take the absolute value of that part's integral before adding (area is always positive).
  • Area bounded by $x=g(y)$, y-axis, and $y=c,y=d$: $A=\displaystyle\int_c^d g(y)\,dy$.

Area between two curves

  • If $f(x)\ge g(x)$ on $[a,b]$: $A=\displaystyle\int_a^b [f(x)-g(x)]\,dx$.
  • Always find intersection points first (solve $f(x)=g(x)$) to get correct limits.

Standard curves & areas

CurveRegion / Area
Circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$Full area $=\pi a^2$; area in first quadrant $=\pi a^2/4$
Ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$Full area $=\pi ab$
Parabola $y^2=4ax$ and line $x=a$Area $=\dfrac{8a^2}{3}$ (both sides of axis)
Line $y=mx$ and parabola $y=x^2$Find intersections, integrate (line $-$ parabola)

Useful integrals for area problems

  • $\displaystyle\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2-x^2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{a}+C$.
  • $\displaystyle\int_0^a\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac{\pi a^2}{4}$ (quarter circle area, a quick shortcut).
  • Power rule: $\displaystyle\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ ($n\ne-1$).

Method / steps

  • 1. Sketch (or mentally visualise) the region. 2. Identify boundaries and points of intersection. 3. Decide whether to integrate w.r.t. $x$ or $y$ (whichever gives simpler limits/integrand). 4. Set up the definite integral of (upper $-$ lower) or (right $-$ left). 5. Evaluate.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 1-2 questions from this chapter, most often the area under a simple parabola/line, the standard circle-quadrant area, or area between a line and a parabola. Memorising the ready-made results for circle, ellipse and parabola areas saves valuable time versus deriving them from scratch.
